description: We are building an AI-powered analytics dashboard that turns complex NASA microgravity combustion data into actionable fire safety intelligence. By integrating automated data ingestion, material flammability ranking, and an intelligent query assistant, our tool helps engineers identify combustion risks and design safer habitats and life-support systems for future Moon and Mars missions.
summary:
We developed AeroFlame_Analytics, an interactive mission-control dashboard and predictive flammability simulator. It ingests 438+ authentic NASA flight records across six major missions (FLEX, BASS-II, Saffire, ACME) to model oxygen partial pressure, limiting oxygen index, airflow, and flame spread across seven exploration environments, including Earth, the ISS, Artemis Lunar Base (34% O2 at 8.2 psi), and Mars.

AeroFlame_Analytics transforms raw Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) data into actionable flight safety tools. Rather than static archives, it provides an empirical combustion engine with real-time 0-G spherical versus 1-G buoyant flame visualizations, automated 0 to 100 fire risk scoring, and flammability boundary mapping, exposing anomalies like the Saffire flammability inversion where materials safe on Earth burn in orbit.

Fire in space is lethal. Without natural buoyant convection, flames form silent spheres and smoke does not rise, blinding ceiling detectors and causing toxic gas accumulation. FLAMEFALL prevents catastrophic failures like Apollo 1 by optimizing life-support atmospheres for Artemis and Mars missions, while advancing life-saving terrestrial spin-offs, including lightweight firefighter breathing apparatus, dual-wavelength transit smoke alarms, and clean water-mist suppression systems.
details:
AeroFlame_Analytics is an interactive aerospace mission-control workstation and predictive fire safety simulator designed to transform raw microgravity combustion data into actionable spacecraft design intelligence.

How It Works & Core Capabilities

  • Authentic Flight Data Ingestion: Harmonizes 438+ NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) flight records across six landmark missions (FLEX droplet combustion, BASS-II solid fuels, Saffire large-scale vehicle burns, and ACME gaseous flames).
  • Empirical Flammability Modeling: Calculates real-time oxygen partial pressure, limiting oxygen index, and flame spread velocities across seven environments—including Earth, ISS, Artemis Lunar Base (34% O2 at 8.2 psi), Mars, and EVA spacesuits.
  • Dual-Chamber Visual Simulator: Dynamically compares tranquil 0-G spherical diffusion flames with 1-G buoyant teardrop plumes under varying ventilation speeds and oxygen fractions.
  • Automated Fire Risk Index: Evaluates material flammability (PMMA, Nomex, Silicone) to generate an immediate 0 to 100 hazard rating and compliance check against NASA-STD-6001.

Engineering Factors Considered

  • The Buoyancy Disconnect: Absence of natural buoyant convection in microgravity traps toxic gases (carbon monoxide) and renders conventional ceiling smoke detectors blind.
  • Terrestrial Testing Limitations: Exposes critical anomalies like the Saffire flammability inversion, where materials that self-extinguish in Earth tests continue burning in orbit due to reduced convective heat loss.
  • Exploration Atmosphere Trade-Offs: Balances crew hypoxia prevention with exponential flammability risks in reduced-pressure, oxygen-enriched lunar habitats.

Technical Implementation & Tools

  • Language & Frameworks: Built entirely in Python using Streamlit, custom HTML5/CSS3, and SVG graphics for an authentic aerospace telemetry aesthetic.
  • Data Processing & Physics: Ingested via native CSV parsers and calculated using NumPy and standard thermodynamic equations.
  • Visualization Engine: Interactive Plotly contour and scatter plots for ventilation curves and d²-law droplet burn rates.

Intended Impact & Earth Spin-offs

FLAMEFALL directly protects deep-space crews on Artemis and Mars missions by preventing catastrophic flashovers before launch. Furthermore, it highlights vital civilian life-safety technologies derived from NASA combustion research:

  • Lightweight SCBA Gear: 30% lighter breathing apparatus for municipal firefighters.
  • Dual-Wavelength Optical Detectors: Advanced sensors that distinguish dust from real smoke in transit tunnels and mines.
  • Fine Water Mist Suppression: Non-toxic, clean suppression systems replacing hazardous Halon across civilian infrastructure.
